questions.stem: Which sequence shows the hierarchical organisation of a multicellular organism, from simplest to most complex?
options: Organs, tissues, cells, organ systems
Cells, organs, tissues, organ systems
Cells, tissues, organs, organ systems
Tissues, cells, organ systems, organs
questions.explanation: Similar cells form tissues, different tissues form an organ, and organs working together form an organ system. Each level depends on the one below it.

questions.stem: The stomach contains muscle, epithelial and nervous tissue working together. At which level of organisation is the stomach?
options: A tissue
A cell
An organ system
An organ
questions.explanation: An organ is made of several tissue types that work together to carry out a function. The stomach is part of the digestive system, which is the organ system.

questions.stem: Which set of features is shared by efficient gas exchange surfaces?
options: Large surface area, thin, moist, with a maintained concentration gradient
Small surface area, thick and dry, with no concentration gradient across it
Large surface area, thick, waxy, with a constant concentration
Small surface area, thin, dry, with an even gas concentration
questions.explanation: A large, thin, moist surface allows gases to dissolve and diffuse quickly, and ventilation and blood flow keep the concentration gradient steep. Thick or dry surfaces slow diffusion.

questions.stem: How does oxygen reach the body cells of an insect?
options: Air enters lungs and oxygen is carried by red blood cells
Air enters spiracles and travels in tracheae directly to the cells
Oxygen is absorbed by the gills and then carried in the haemolymph
Oxygen diffuses through the thick exoskeleton into the blood
questions.explanation: Spiracles open into a branching network of tracheae and tracheoles that deliver air close to every cell, so the circulatory system does not need to carry oxygen. Insects have no lungs, and their exoskeleton limits gas exchange.

questions.stem: In fish gills, water flows over the lamellae in the opposite direction to the blood flowing through them. What is the advantage?
options: The gradient is lost halfway along, so the fish wastes less energy pumping
A concentration gradient is kept along the whole lamella, so more oxygen is absorbed
Water and blood mix together, so oxygen moves straight into the fish's blood
The blood loses oxygen to the water, and this keeps the gills cool in warm conditions
questions.explanation: With countercurrent flow, blood always meets water with a higher oxygen concentration than itself, so oxygen diffuses in along the full length of the lamella. With parallel flow, the two would reach equilibrium partway and uptake would stop.

questions.stem: Which features of mammalian alveoli make them efficient for gas exchange?
options: Huge total surface area, walls one cell thick and a dense capillary network
Thick muscular walls and a waxy lining that keeps the inner surface completely dry
A small number of large air sacs with very few blood vessels
Hard, rigid walls that stop air moving in and out of the lungs
questions.explanation: Millions of alveoli give a very large surface area, the thin walls give a short diffusion distance, and the capillaries carry oxygen away and bring carbon dioxide, keeping gradients steep. The alveolar surface is moist, not dry.

questions.stem: Earthworms exchange gases through their skin. Why must they live in moist environments?
options: Their skin produces oxygen only when it is wet
Dry air would make their gills collapse together
Gases must dissolve in a moist surface layer before diffusing in
Moist soil contains much more oxygen than the air above the ground
questions.explanation: Gases diffuse across a gas exchange surface in solution, so the skin must stay moist; a dried-out earthworm cannot take in oxygen. Earthworms have no gills.

questions.stem: Why can an animal that relies only on its skin for gas exchange not grow large and active?
options: Skin can exchange carbon dioxide but never oxygen, whatever its area
Large animals need no oxygen, so the skin stops working as they grow
Its surface area to volume ratio falls as it grows, so skin cannot supply enough oxygen
Its surface area to volume ratio rises as it grows, so it then loses far too much oxygen
questions.explanation: As body size increases, volume (and oxygen demand) grows faster than surface area, so the skin alone cannot meet the needs of a large, active animal. Large active animals have internal surfaces such as lungs or gills.

questions.stem: How does a gastrovascular cavity, as in a jellyfish or hydra, differ from an alimentary canal?
options: It has two openings, with food moving in one direction only
It has many specialised regions, such as a separate stomach and intestines
It digests food only inside cells, never in any internal cavity
It has one opening used for both taking in food and removing wastes
questions.explanation: A gastrovascular cavity has a single opening, so food enters and wastes leave by the same route. An alimentary canal has a mouth and an anus, allowing one-way flow through specialised regions.

questions.stem: What is the main advantage of an alimentary canal with two openings over a gastrovascular cavity?
options: Food can enter and leave through the same opening at any time
No enzymes are needed, because food is broken down by muscle alone
Food is absorbed straight into every body cell without being digested
Food moves one way through regions specialised for different stages
questions.explanation: One-way flow lets different regions carry out ingestion, digestion, absorption and egestion in sequence, and the animal can eat while still digesting earlier meals. A single opening limits this.

questions.stem: Why do herbivores generally have a longer alimentary canal than carnivores of similar size?
options: Carnivores absorb nutrients through the skin instead of the gut
Plant material is high in cellulose and takes longer to digest
Meat is high in cellulose, which needs a very short digestive tract
Herbivores eat less often, so food must be stored for longer
questions.explanation: Cellulose is hard to break down and needs a long time and the help of microbes, so herbivores have long guts, often with large fermentation chambers. Animal protein is more easily digested, so carnivores have shorter, simpler guts.

questions.stem: Rabbits and horses have a large caecum. What is its function?
options: Housing microbes that ferment cellulose from the plants eaten
Producing hydrochloric acid to kill bacteria in meat
Absorbing most of the water from undigested food
Storing bile that is used to digest fats and proteins
questions.explanation: Animals cannot make the enzyme that digests cellulose, but microbes in the caecum ferment it, releasing products the animal can absorb. Carnivores have a small or reduced caecum.

questions.stem: A skull has sharp, pointed canines and blade-like cheek teeth, and the animal's gut is short with a small caecum. What is its diet most likely to be?
options: Leaves
Seeds
Meat
Grass
questions.explanation: Long canines and shearing cheek teeth suit catching and slicing flesh, and a short gut with a small caecum suits easily digested animal protein. Grass and leaf eaters have flat grinding teeth and long guts.

questions.stem: Why do grazing herbivores such as kangaroos and sheep have broad, flat molars?
options: To grind tough plant material, breaking open cell walls
To slice through flesh and crack open the bones of prey
To hold and kill prey before it is swallowed whole
To store food in the mouth until it can be swallowed
questions.explanation: Grinding breaks plant cell walls and increases the surface area for microbes and enzymes to act on. Slicing flesh is the job of the blade-like teeth of carnivores.

questions.stem: What is the main difference between an open and a closed circulatory system?
options: In an open system, blood stays in vessels; in a closed system, fluid bathes the organs directly
An open system has no heart at all, while a closed system always has four heart chambers
An open system carries oxygen to all cells, while a closed system carries only nutrients
In an open system, fluid bathes the organs directly; in a closed system, blood stays in vessels
questions.explanation: In open systems, such as those of insects, haemolymph is pumped into a body cavity and flows around the organs. In closed systems, such as those of vertebrates and earthworms, blood is confined to vessels.

questions.stem: Why can a closed circulatory system support a higher metabolic rate than an open system?
options: Blood is under higher pressure and flows faster to the tissues
Blood moves slowly, giving each cell more time to absorb oxygen
Fluid bathes all organs directly, so no vessels slow the flow
Closed systems carry no oxygen, so they need less energy to run
questions.explanation: Confining blood to vessels lets the heart maintain higher pressure, delivering oxygen and nutrients quickly to active tissues. Open systems work at low pressure and suit animals with lower demands or other ways of delivering oxygen.

questions.stem: Insects are often very active, yet they have an open circulatory system. How is this possible?
options: Insects do not respire, so their cells need no oxygen at all
Insects absorb oxygen from food, so they do not exchange gases
Their tracheal system delivers oxygen directly, so the blood need not carry it
Their open system runs at a higher pressure than any closed system
questions.explanation: Because tracheae carry air straight to the tissues, insect haemolymph mainly transports nutrients and wastes rather than oxygen. This lets a low-pressure open system meet their needs.

questions.stem: A fish has a two-chambered heart, and blood passes through the heart once for each circuit of the body. What type of circulation is this?
options: Open circulation
Pulmonary circulation
Single circulation
Double circulation
questions.explanation: In single circulation blood is pumped from the heart to the gills and then on to the body before returning. Mammals and birds have double circulation, with separate lung and body circuits.

questions.stem: Why is double circulation an advantage for mammals and birds compared with single circulation?
options: Blood returns to the heart after the lungs, so it is pumped to the body at high pressure
Blood passes through the lungs twice, so it carries twice as much oxygen
Oxygenated and deoxygenated blood mix fully, so that all tissues receive the very same blood
The body circuit runs at low pressure, so the heart needs less energy to pump
questions.explanation: Blood loses pressure in the lung capillaries, so returning it to the heart for a second pump delivers it to the body quickly and at high pressure, supporting high metabolic rates and endothermy. A four-chambered heart also keeps oxygenated and deoxygenated blood separate.

questions.stem: Nitrogenous wastes are produced mainly from the breakdown of which nutrient?
options: Proteins
Carbohydrates
Fats
Vitamins
questions.explanation: Amino acids from proteins contain nitrogen; when they are broken down, the nitrogen-containing amino group is removed and converted to ammonia, urea or uric acid. Carbohydrates and fats contain no nitrogen.

questions.stem: Which list gives the main wastes that animals must excrete?
options: Water, starch, cellulose and amino acids
Carbon dioxide, water, nitrogenous compounds and salts
Oxygen, glucose, amino acids and fatty acids
Carbon dioxide, glucose, oxygen and vitamins
questions.explanation: Metabolism produces carbon dioxide, excess water, nitrogenous wastes from protein breakdown and excess salts, all of which must be removed. Glucose and amino acids are useful nutrients that the body keeps.

questions.stem: How do most aquatic animals get rid of their nitrogenous waste?
options: They release it as a gas through specialised lungs
They release ammonia directly into the surrounding water
They store uric acid in their tissues for months at a time
They convert all of it into glucose for later use
questions.explanation: Ammonia is toxic but very soluble, and in water it diffuses away across gills or the body surface and is quickly diluted. Terrestrial animals need specialised mechanisms, such as kidneys, to deal with nitrogenous waste.

questions.stem: Why do terrestrial animals need specialised excretory organs such as kidneys or Malpighian tubules?
options: Wastes cannot simply diffuse away into water, so they must be removed while water is conserved
Terrestrial animals produce no carbon dioxide, so another waste must be removed instead
On land, ammonia diffuses away into the air, so excretory organs are needed to collect it back
Terrestrial animals take in no salt, so their organs must make salt to stay in balance
questions.explanation: On land there is no surrounding water to dilute and carry away ammonia, and water is precious, so animals convert nitrogenous waste to less toxic forms and excrete it with controlled water loss. Kidneys in vertebrates and Malpighian tubules in insects do this.

questions.stem: In vascular plants, how are gases exchanged between the leaf and the air?
options: Through the phloem, which pumps gases to the leaves
Through root hairs, which pass gases up the stem
Through stomata and the plant surface, by diffusion
Through the xylem, which carries gases from the roots
questions.explanation: Gases diffuse in and out through stomata and across plant surfaces, and then through air spaces inside the leaf. Unlike in many animals, the transport system is not used to move gases.

questions.stem: Which cells open and close each stoma on a leaf, and how?
options: A pair of guard cells that change shape as they gain or lose water
The xylem vessels, which push the pore open with water pressure
The phloem, which fills the pore with sugar to keep it closed
The cuticle, which melts in the heat to cover the pore
questions.explanation: When guard cells take up water they swell and bend apart, opening the pore; when they lose water they close it. This lets plants balance carbon dioxide uptake against water loss.

questions.stem: How do the cells in a woody stem obtain oxygen for respiration?
options: By diffusion through lenticels and air spaces in the bark
From oxygen carried up from the roots in the phloem
From oxygen dissolved in xylem sap pumped from the leaves
From photosynthesis, as every stem cell makes all it needs
questions.explanation: Lenticels are small pores in bark that let gases diffuse into the living tissues of the stem. Gases are not carried by the vascular system in plants.

questions.stem: What does the xylem transport in a vascular plant?
options: Carbon dioxide from the roots up to the leaves
Water and mineral nutrients from the roots to the leaves
Sugars from the leaves to the roots and growing tips
Oxygen from the leaves to every cell of the plant
questions.explanation: Xylem carries water and dissolved mineral ions upwards from the roots. Sugars made in photosynthesis are carried in the phloem.

questions.stem: What is the main force that pulls water up the xylem of a tall tree?
options: Transpiration: evaporation from the leaves draws water up the xylem
Translocation: sugars are actively pumped up the xylem from the roots
Root pressure alone, pushing water to the top of the tallest trees
Gravity, which draws water down from the leaves to the roots
questions.explanation: As water evaporates from leaf cells and diffuses out through stomata, it creates a tension that pulls the column of water up through the xylem. Root pressure contributes, but it can only push water a short distance.

questions.stem: In xylem transport, what do cohesion and adhesion refer to?
options: Cohesion: water attracted to xylem walls; adhesion: water molecules attracted to each other
Cohesion: sugars sticking to water; adhesion: minerals sticking to the root hairs
Cohesion: water moving by osmosis; adhesion: water moving by active transport
Cohesion: water molecules attracted to each other; adhesion: water attracted to xylem walls
questions.explanation: Hydrogen bonds hold water molecules together (cohesion), so the column is pulled up as one, and attract water to the walls of the narrow vessels (adhesion), producing capillary action. Together these help maintain an unbroken column.

questions.stem: A stem is cut close to the ground, and sap continues to ooze from the stump for some time. What causes this?
options: Transpiration pull, as the leaves on the stump still evaporate water
Translocation, as sugars are pushed down from the leaves to the roots
Capillary action alone, lifting water out of the stump against gravity
Root pressure, from ions pumped into the xylem drawing water in by osmosis
questions.explanation: Root cells actively move mineral ions into the xylem, lowering its water potential, so water enters by osmosis and pushes up the stem. With the shoot removed, there are no leaves to provide transpiration pull.

questions.stem: A potometer shows a leafy shoot taking up water fastest on a warm, dry, windy day. What is the best explanation?
options: Photosynthesis is slowest, so the shoot stores more water in its cells
Root pressure is highest, so more water is pushed up from below
Humidity is highest, so water vapour moves into the leaves from the air
Evaporation from the leaves is fastest, so transpiration pulls more water up
questions.explanation: Warmth, dry air and wind all steepen the water vapour gradient between the leaf and the air, increasing transpiration, which pulls more water through the shoot. A cut shoot in a potometer has no roots, so root pressure plays no part.

questions.stem: Why are xylem vessels well suited to carrying water?
options: They are short cells with thick end walls that stop water moving
They are hollow, dead tubes strengthened with lignin and joined end to end
They are living cells with many mitochondria to pump water upwards
They are filled with cytoplasm that actively absorbs water from the wet soil
questions.explanation: Mature xylem vessels have no contents and no end walls, forming continuous tubes, and lignin stops them collapsing under the tension of the water column. Water moves passively, so no living contents are needed.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes translocation in vascular plants?
options: The exchange of gases through the lenticels of a woody stem
The transport of sugars and some mineral nutrients in the phloem
The transport of water from the roots to the leaves in the xylem
The loss of water vapour from leaves through the stomata
questions.explanation: Translocation moves the products of photosynthesis, mainly sucrose, and some mineral nutrients through the phloem's sieve tubes. Water movement in the xylem and loss of vapour through stomata are part of transpiration.

questions.stem: How does the direction of transport in the phloem differ from that in the xylem?
options: Phloem moves sugars only upwards, from the roots to the leaves
Phloem moves water only downwards, from the leaves to the roots
Phloem moves minerals only upwards, in the same way as xylem
Phloem moves sugars from sources to sinks, which can be up or down
questions.explanation: Sugars travel from where they are made or stored (sources, such as leaves) to where they are used or stored (sinks, such as roots, fruits and growing tips), so flow can go either way. Xylem carries water upwards only.

questions.stem: A ring of bark, including the phloem but not the xylem, is removed from a tree trunk. After some weeks the bark just above the ring swells. Why?
options: Sugars moving up from the roots build up above the ring
Minerals from the soil build up as the xylem is blocked
Sugars moving down in the phloem build up above the ring
Water moving up in the xylem builds up above the ring
questions.explanation: Removing the phloem blocks the downward movement of sugars from the leaves, so they accumulate above the cut and the tissue swells. The xylem is intact, so water still reaches the leaves.

questions.stem: Which statement about phloem tissue is correct?
options: Its sieve tubes are living cells, supported by companion cells
Its tubes are dead, hollow cells strengthened with lignin
It carries water upwards only, driven by transpiration
It carries gases from the stomata to the roots
questions.explanation: Phloem sieve tube elements are living cells linked by sieve plates, and companion cells supply the energy needed to load sugars. Dead, lignified tubes describe xylem.
